newsitem.title: FRANCE: Embarrassed French government silent on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Embarrassed French government silent on Zaire.

text.p: France kept silence on Saturday on the takeover of Zaire by rebel leader Laurent Kabila, seen as an embarrassing setback for the conservative government at the height of an election campaign.
A foreign ministry spokesman had no comment as Kabila proclaimed he was taking over as head of state from France's ally Mobutu Sese Seko.
Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin had been prompt on Friday to bring up Mobutu's flight to his home village of Gbadolite into the campaign for the May 25/June 1 parliamentary election.
"What is happening in Zaire certainly seals in a way the failure of France's African policy," he said.
The ministry spokesman said he had no indications of whether the ailing Mobutu might seek exile in France where he has made several stays over the past few months.
Analysts said the French government would not be keen to give him shelter at least until after the election for fear his presence should become a campaign issue.
Mobutu, who regained Paris' favours three years ago, made long stays in his smart French Riviera mansion as he recovered from cancer surgery while rebels were gradually taking over his country.

France's past support to Rwanda's ousted Hutu-led government weighed heavily on its policy which seemed hopelessly overtaken by events since Kabila's Rwanda-backed, Tutsi-led rebels took over a swathe of eastern Zaire last October.

Paris' bid to send a multinational force to eastern Zaire to protect Rwandan Hutu refugees was approved by the United Nations despite U.S. reluctance, only to be dropped as a large number of refugees returned home and the rebels feared the force would be used to keep Mobutu in power.

Like other major powers, France had ostracised Mobutu for his autocratic rule and record on corruption and human rights. A French Socialist cabinet minister once described him as "a walking safe in a leopard-skin hat". He was at one point barred from entering France and staying at his Riviera mansion.

But he regained Paris' favour when he allowed French troops to use bases in Zaire for their 1994 Turquoise operation to stop revenge massacres of Hutus in Rwanda following the genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
French officials, saying Paris was working with Washington to ensure a peaceful transition in Zaire, have sought to play down France's diplomatic isolation through the crisis.

But it was clear it played little role, and the changeover in one of the world's biggest French-speaking countries marked a sharp loss of influence in a continent Paris has long regarded as its backyard.

Ironically, the influential French daily Le Monde commented on Saturday, France has few economic interests in the mineral-rich former Belgian colony where the biggest investors are Belgium, the United States and South Africa.
"The mistake of sticking by Mobutu over the past few years was all the worse," it said.
